response:
Verified the three findings against the fixture before judging — all three reproduce on disk (`docs/` contains only `billing.md`, `commands.md`, `teams.md`; there is no `setup.md`).

## Verdict

| # | Finding | Charge | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|
| `crime_00033` | `docs_code_drift` — `docs/teams.md` | Docs-Code Drift | **Block merge** (scoped to changed docs) |
| `crime_00007` | `route_metadata_drift` — `/settings/billing` | Route Metadata Drift | **Warn** → block if the PR touches the route or its nav |
| `crime_00006` | `duplicated_navigation_source` — `/settings/billing` | Duplicated Navigation Source | **Warn** → block on the same trigger; fix with `crime_00007` |

Note the inversion: the finding crimes ranks *lowest* (`agent_risk` 0.24, `severity: low`) is the one I'd block on, and the two it ranks highest (0.38 each) I'd let through with a warning. Gating policy keys off **confidence × fix cost**, not severity — a merge gate has to be cheap and unambiguous or teams route around it.

---

### `crime_00033` — docs_code_drift → **block**

> `docs/teams.md:5 → ./setup.md (not found)`

Confirmed: `docs/teams.md` line 5 reads `See the [setup guide](./setup.md) to invite the first members.` and `docs/setup.md` does not exist.

Block because this is the only one of the three where the detector isn't exercising judgement — `confidence: 0.9` understates it; the file either resolves or it doesn't. There's no false-positive story, no design debate, and the fix is one line (restore the file, or repoint the link). Blocking costs a contributor ~30 seconds.

The failure mode is also the sharpest of the three for agents: an agent told to "follow the setup guide" gets nothing back and will confabulate the invite flow rather than report a dead link.

**Scope it to changed files** — `crimes scan --changed --fail-on low` — so an unrelated PR isn't held hostage by pre-existing rot in `docs/`. If you want the whole doc tree clean, that's a `crimes baseline save` + burn-down, not a merge gate.

### `crime_00007` — route_metadata_drift → **warn**

> route path: `/settings/billing` · component: `PricingPage` · `metadata.title`: `Plans` · `<title>`: `Subscription` · nav: `Plans` / `Billing`

Confirmed in `src/routes/settings/billing.tsx` — four names for one destination in a 13-line file.

This is the highest-value finding of the three and still shouldn't block. `confidence: 0.65` is the lowest in the report for a reason: the detector can't distinguish accidental drift from legitimate divergence. A URL path is a stable identifier and a `<title>` is user-facing copy; those *should* be free to differ. Marketing may deliberately want "Subscription" in the browser tab while the IA calls the section Billing. A gate that can't tell those apart trains people to ignore it.

What makes it real here isn't the count, it's that no two sources agree and no one is marked canonical — a `Pricing`/`Plans`/`Billing`/`Subscription` split means an agent asked to "rename the billing page" will find one of four and stop.

**Escalate to block when the diff touches `src/routes/settings/billing.tsx` or either nav file.** That's precisely the edit where an agent updates one label and strands three, and at that moment the reviewer already has the context loaded.

### `crime_00006` — duplicated_navigation_source → **warn**

> `src/nav/registry.ts` label: `Plans` · `src/nav/sidebar.ts` label: `Billing`

Both files exist and both self-document as fixtures that disagree. Genuine two-sources-of-truth problem, and the suggested action is honest about the cost — `"risk": "medium"`, because consolidating nav sources is an architectural change.

Don't block: forcing a nav refactor into whatever unrelated PR happens to trip the detector is how gates get disabled. Warn, and if you want it fixed, file it as its own change.

**These two are one defect, not two.** `crime_00007`'s evidence list *contains* `crime_00006`'s evidence — the two conflicting nav labels are cited as two of the four competing names. Gating them independently double-counts a single root cause, and fixing `crime_00006` (pick one label, one source) clears roughly half of `crime_00007` for free. Treat them as one work item: name the destination canonically, make one nav file the source, derive the rest.

---

## Wider context worth flagging

The three findings you named aren't isolated — the scan shows the IA is fragmented repo-wide:

- **`crime_00029/30/31`** (`orphaned_destination`): `/account/subscription`, `/team`, `/workspace/members` are all unreachable from nav, docs, or imports. Combined with `crime_00006`, the picture is that nav isn't a source of truth for this app at all — it covers 2 of 5 routes.
- **`crime_00019`** (`concept_alias_drift`): four aliases — `account`, `organisation`, `team`, `workspace` — for the tenant concept across 5 files, including the orphaned routes. The naming problem in `crime_00007` is a local instance of a repo-wide vocabulary problem.

Ignore each of those individually; they're `confidence: 0.65` and blocking a merge on "this route isn't linked yet" would break every stacked-PR workflow. But if you're fixing the billing route's naming, do it as part of choosing canonical vocabulary once, or you'll be back here for `/team` next month.

## Encoding it

```bash
crimes scan --changed --fail-on low --format json
```

Then suppress the two IA warnings with recorded reasons so they stay visible in review without gating:

```bash
crimes ignore duplicated_navigation_source::src/nav/registry.ts \
  --reason "Nav consolidation tracked separately; blocking unrelated PRs on an architectural refactor"
crimes ignore route_metadata_drift::src/routes/settings/billing.tsx \
  --reason "Canonical-name decision pending with nav consolidation; same root cause"
```

`--fail-on low` is aggressive on the changed set, but with the two IA findings suppressed it resolves to "no dead doc links in files you touched" — which is the gate I'd actually want. Suppressed findings never trip a `--fail-on` gate, and the reasons stay in `.crimes/suppressions.json` for the reviewer.
